topic: Repatriation Cover: The Line Consulates Check That Cheap Policies Leave Out
metaTitle: Repatriation Cover: The Line Schengen Consulates Check
metaDescription: Schengen insurance must pay for repatriation, not just EUR 30,000 of medical care. Here is how to read your policy schedule before you hand the visa file in.
excerpt: Article 15 of the EU Visa Code asks Schengen insurance to do three things, and repatriation is the one budget policies quietly omit. This guide shows you how to read a policy schedule and spot the gap before your appointment, and why insurance is a different kind of document from a flight reservation.
quickAnswer: Repatriation cover is the line consulates check and cheap policies leave out. Article 15 of the EU Visa Code requires travel medical insurance of at least EUR 30,000, valid across all 27 Schengen states, covering urgent medical attention, emergency hospital treatment, repatriation for medical reasons and repatriation in the event of death. If your schedule names no repatriation benefit, the policy fails.
content:
Schengen insurance has to clear three bars at once, and applicants usually only check the first one. Article 15 of the EU Visa Code asks for cover of at least EUR 30,000, valid across every member state, that pays for emergency medical treatment and for repatriation on medical grounds or in the event of death. Cheap policies hit the headline number and thin out the repatriation limb, which is exactly where a file gets handed back across the counter.

What does Article 15 of the EU Visa Code actually require?

Article 15 of Regulation (EC) No 810/2009, the EU Visa Code, says applicants for a short-stay visa must prove they hold adequate and valid travel medical insurance. The cover has to deal with expenses arising from repatriation for medical reasons, urgent medical attention, emergency hospital treatment, or death, during the stay on the territory of the member states.

The minimum is EUR 30,000, and the insurance has to be valid throughout the territory of the member states for the whole intended stay or transit. The European Commission's own summary for applicants puts it in plainer words: medical insurance covering emergency medical care, hospitalisation and repatriation, including in the event of death.

Read that list again. It is not one benefit with a big number attached. It is a set of four things the policy has to be able to pay for, and repatriation appears twice, once for medical reasons and once for death.

At a glance

RequirementWhat the rule saysSource
Minimum coverAt least EUR 30,000Article 15, EU Visa Code
Geographic validityValid throughout the territory of the member states, all 27 Schengen countriesArticle 15, EU Visa Code
Medical limbUrgent medical attention and emergency hospital treatmentArticle 15, EU Visa Code
Repatriation limbRepatriation for medical reasons, and repatriation in the event of deathEuropean Commission, applying for a Schengen visa
Period of validityThe entire period of the intended stay or transitArticle 15, EU Visa Code
Where claims must be payableClaims recoverable in a member stateArticle 15, EU Visa Code
Proof acceptedA policy document or certificate. Insurance card copies are refused by some visa centresVFS Global UAE checklist

What should be on the policy schedule before you submit?

Do not read the sales page. Read the schedule, which is the one or two page document with your name, the dates and the benefit table on it. That is the page the visa officer reads too.

Work down this list before your appointment:

  • Your name and passport number, spelled exactly as on the passport you are submitting.
  • Dates that start on or before your first Schengen entry and end on or after your exit, with a day of margin at each end.
  • A cover amount of EUR 30,000 or more, stated in euros, not in dirhams or dollars with a note about exchange rates.
  • The words "Schengen" or a list naming the member states, or a statement that the policy is valid throughout the territory of the Schengen states.
  • A named benefit for repatriation for medical reasons, sometimes written as medical repatriation or medical evacuation and repatriation.
  • A named benefit for repatriation of mortal remains, which is the death limb of the rule.
  • An emergency assistance number that works from abroad, with a 24 hour line.
  • The insurer's name and a policy number, so the consulate can tell who carries the risk.

If any of those eight lines is missing, assume the file is short and fix it before you walk in. Our Schengen travel insurance is genuine AXA-issued cover from AED 30, written to the EUR 30,000 minimum and valid across all 27 member states, and the schedule arrives with the benefits named on it.

Why do cheap policies leave repatriation out?

Because repatriation is the expensive part. An air ambulance out of Europe, or the transport of remains home to the UAE or on to a family's home country, runs into tens of thousands of euros on a single claim. Emergency treatment is capped and predictable, but a repatriation is one large, awkward payout.

So budget plans do one of three things. They omit repatriation altogether and lean on a big medical headline. They include it but cap it at a token amount, a few thousand euros, which does not buy an air ambulance. Or they bury it inside an assistance service that arranges the transport but does not pay for it.

None of these is a scam, and the plans are usually legitimate insurance for what they say they cover. The problem is that none of them answers Article 15, and the sales page will not tell you that. Only the schedule does.

Why do policies get rejected at the visa centre?

Rejections at the counter are mostly mechanical, not judgement calls. The clerk is working through a checklist, and the same handful of faults come up again and again:

  • No repatriation benefit named. The cover total is fine, the words are not there, and the document fails the check.
  • A repatriation cap far below the medical cover. Consulates that look closely treat a token cap as not covering the risk.
  • Cover under EUR 30,000, or quoted in another currency so nobody can tell.
  • Country list short of the full member states. A single country policy fails even if you only plan to visit that country, because the rule asks for validity throughout the territory.
  • Dates that do not cover the whole trip, usually a policy that ends on the departure date rather than after it.
  • An insurance card or a screenshot instead of the policy. The VFS Global checklist used in the UAE states outright that card copies are not accepted.
  • Name mismatches between the policy and the passport, which are common when a name has four parts and an insurer's form has two boxes.

Getting handed the file back is not a refusal, and it is not recorded as one. It does cost you the appointment, though, and in a busy season in Dubai or Abu Dhabi the next slot might be weeks away.

If you would rather not audit a policy line by line, buying AXA-issued cover built for the Schengen requirement removes the guesswork. Check the policy wording for the exact benefit limits, because those vary by plan and the schedule is always the authority.

Is insurance the same kind of document as a flight reservation?

No, and this is worth being precise about, because people lump the two together as "visa paperwork".

A flight reservation is evidence of a plan. It shows a real seat held under a live booking reference, on a route and a date, so the consulate can see your intended travel. Article 14 of the Visa Code asks for evidence of travel arrangements, not for a paid fare, which is why a reservation answers the requirement. The UAE checklist says it plainly: a copy of a flight ticket or flight reservation, including the return flight.

Insurance is not evidence of anything. It is a live contract. If you fall down a flight of stairs in Milan, someone has to pay the hospital, and the policy is the instrument that does it. That is why the rule is written in terms of what the cover pays for rather than what it proves.

The practical consequence is simple. A reservation can be held, released, reissued with new dates and kept short. A policy cannot be faked or half-issued, and there is no cheap version of it that still functions. You buy the real thing or you do not have it.

Do multiple entry applicants need something different?

Yes, in one respect. Article 15 requires an applicant for a multiple entry visa to prove cover for the period of the first intended visit, and to sign a declaration that they understand they need to hold insurance for later stays as well.

So the policy you buy for the application does not have to stretch across the whole validity of a five year visa, which would be absurd. It has to cover trip one, and you have to buy travel insurance again before trip two. Some consulates in the UAE hand you that declaration as a separate form at the counter.

Worth knowing too: Article 15 lets a consulate waive the insurance requirement for certain applicants, for example where cover is assumed to exist because of the person's professional situation. Do not assume you are in that group. Ask the consulate directly if you think you are.

What does the whole file cost from the UAE?

Two kinds of fee sit in a Schengen file, and it helps to keep them apart. The visa fee is governmental and goes to the consulate. Everything else is a service cost.

ItemCostWho charges it
Schengen visa fee, adultEUR 90Governmental, set by the EU since 11 June 2024
Schengen visa fee, child aged 6 to under 12EUR 45Governmental
Visa centre service feeVaries by country and centreThe visa centre, check its own published fee list
AXA travel insurance meeting the EUR 30,000 minimumFrom AED 30The Dummy Ticket AE
Flight reservation for the fileFrom AED 49The Dummy Ticket AE

The visa fee figures come from the European Commission's announcement of the fee increase on 11 June 2024. Visa centre service fees are published per country and per centre, so check the one handling your application rather than a general figure.

Against a EUR 90 fee and the cost of the trip, the insurance is the cheapest line on the list and the easiest one to get wrong. Take the twenty minutes to read the schedule, or buy cover that already names what Article 15 asks for and spend the twenty minutes on your bank statements instead, which is where refusals actually happen.

faqs.question: Does Schengen insurance have to cover repatriation?
faqs.answer: Yes. Article 15 of the EU Visa Code requires cover for repatriation on medical grounds and in the event of death, alongside urgent medical attention and emergency hospital treatment. A policy with EUR 30,000 of medical cover but no repatriation benefit does not meet the rule.

faqs.question: How do I check my policy covers repatriation?
faqs.answer: Open the policy schedule, not the sales page, and look for a benefit named repatriation for medical reasons and a second named repatriation of mortal remains. If neither phrase appears in the benefit table, treat the policy as short and replace it.

faqs.question: Is EUR 30,000 of cover enough on its own?
faqs.answer: No. EUR 30,000 is the minimum amount, not the whole test. The policy also has to be valid throughout the territory of the member states, run for the entire intended stay, and pay for both emergency treatment and repatriation.

faqs.question: Can I use a single country policy for a Schengen visa?
faqs.answer: No. Article 15 requires the insurance to be valid throughout the territory of the member states, so cover limited to one country fails even if you only plan to visit that country. The schedule should say Schengen or list the member states.

faqs.question: Is travel insurance the same as a flight reservation in a visa file?
faqs.answer: No. A flight reservation is evidence of a travel plan under a live booking reference. Insurance is a live contract that pays a hospital or an air ambulance if something goes wrong. Consulates ask for both, for different reasons.
